newsitem.title: JAPAN: FORECAST-Japan stocks underpinned but range-bound.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-Japan stocks underpinned but range-bound.

text.p: Tokyo stocks are expected to be range-bound this week, with a small handful of high-tech issues underpinning the market continuing to rally, brokers said.
"Stocks tumbled on Friday and it remains to be seen if public funds step in to hunt for bargains," a fund manager at a foreign investment trust said.
"If bargain hunting doesn't appear, the indices are likely to hover within a narrow range, only the range will be lower than in the past few weeks."
On Friday, a hiccup in the Tokyo stock exchange's electronic system trading halted trade of 1,702 issues, 108 of which are included in the Nikkei average, in the morning.
Arbitrage-linked selling emerged when trade resumed after the lunch break.

Futures selling accelerated in mid-afternoon, fuelled by news that domestic car sales fell for the fourth straight month on a year-on-year basis, showing that the economy was not recovering as investors had hoped.

The Nikkei 225 suffered its sixth-largest point drop this year as a result, ending down 527.05 points, or 2.59 percent, at 19,804.38. It was its first close below 20,000 since July 11, when it ended at 19,875.49.

"The fall on Friday was due largely to extraordinary reasons and does not necessarily mean that the Nikkei average has entered a down trend," said Hideyuki Ohkoshi, of Yamaichi Securities. "Support is seen at the July 9 low of 19,495.85."
Brokers said the two-tiered appearance of the market was likely to continue, as investors moved to buy issues that are competitive internationally.
"The yen is weak against the dollar, which is good for those high-tech firms that are competitive with overseas firms," said Noboru Yorita, Tachibana Securities' general manager.
"The only cloud is the anxiety over the U.S. stock market bull run, which could falter any day and drag blue chips with it."

Brokers said they were keeping an eye out for further developments in the brokerage scandal after Tokyo prosecutors raided Yamaichi Securities on suspicions that it was involved in the racketeer scandal that ensnared Nomura Securities.

"The worst is over for Nomura, but the investigation is just starting for Yamaichi and no one knows what will happen," one broker said. "It is financially weaker than Nomura, which means it may have more difficulty if penalties are administered."
There was also concern about the health of the Japanese economy, market sources said.
Jason James, research director at HSBC James Capel, said that compared to June, the P/E ratio estimates for issues included in the Nikkei 225 index had declined by about five percent.
"Following events such as constructor Tada Corp filing for court protection, wariness is growing over the financial state of firms," he said.
"Judging from the glum car sales figures and forecasts for a cool summer, there is a chance that the P/E downward revision could continue until the interim earnings are announced."
